title: Institutional Holdings of Bitcoin ETPs Reach New All-Time High
summary: 13F filings show wealth channel portion of ETP ownership reaches 40%.
body_markdown:
## Introduction


Institutions returned to U.S. spot bitcoin exchange-traded products (ETPs) as net buyers in the third quarter of 2026.


Investment managers that file Form 13F with the SEC added the equivalent of 49,229 BTC, net of sales. That is the most since Q2 2025 and more than the 47,054 they had sold over the previous three quarters. Filers reported a record 356,491 BTC-equivalent ($29.78 billion) as of Sept. 30, 2026. Half of the net addition came from advisors and wealth platforms, which hold more of the funds than at any point since the ETPs launched in January 2024, both in bitcoin terms and as a share of institutional holdings. The continued accumulation in Q3 (July 1 through Sept. 30) occurred while bitcoin traded between its bear market low of $57,717 on July 1 and a Sept. 21 recent hit of $87,397.


*This report covers only holders of U.S. spot bitcoin ETPs, not foreign-issued vehicles.*


## Key Takeaways


-


**Advisors and wealth platforms are at record highs on every measure.** The category, which covers registered investment advisors (RIAs), wealth managers, wirehouses and broker-dealer platforms, reported 144,307 BTC-equivalent as of Sept. 30, 2026. That is 40.5% of all 13F-reported spot bitcoin ETP holdings and 11.2% of all the bitcoin in the funds, and each figure is the highest in the series. Holdings have grown for nine straight quarters and are 3.3x their level on March 31, 2024; the one decline came in Q2 2024, the second quarter after launch. The category's share of 13F holdings has risen for five straight quarters, from 22.2% on June 30, 2025, after slipping in three of the earlier quarters.


-


**They have also been the steadiest buyers.** Advisors and wealth platforms have been net buyers for nine consecutive quarters and account for 100,003 of the 179,300 BTC-equivalent that all filers added from Q2 2024 through Q3 2026. During the three quarters of net institutional selling that ended June 30, 2026, they added 32,706 while basis and relative-value hedge funds sold 54,683.


-


**The wirehouses drove the quarter.** The category added a record 24,838 BTC-equivalent, of which 22,728 came from wirehouses and broker-dealer platforms, led by Wells Fargo (+14,636), Bank of America (+7,201) and Morgan Stanley (+2,875). We then split those firms by business unit. Holdings at their advisor and brokerage arms rose to 43,583 from 30,978, and holdings at their dealer and trading units rose to 12,551 from 3,982, most of it at Bank of America.


-


**Wells Fargo is the largest 13F holder for the first time.** It reported 30,553 BTC-equivalent ($2.55 billion), nearly double the 15,931 it held on June 30, 2026, and passed Jane Street, which led a quarter earlier. No wealth platform had ranked first before: Millennium Management was the largest holder in every quarter from Q1 2024 through Q1 2026.


-


**Breadth recovered, but a few large firms drove the net addition of bitcoin.** The number of managers holding a spot bitcoin fund rose by 191 to 2,166, the first increase after two quarters of decline: 358 managers that held no position a quarter earlier reported one and 167 dropped out. The newcomers are small, with 9,554 BTC-equivalent among them. The 50 largest holders added a net 59,578, and all other managers combined, including those that left, were net sellers of 10,349.


-


**Form 13F filers hold 27.6% of the bitcoin in the ETPs.** That is up from 24.8% on June 30, 2026, and just under the high of 27.7% on Dec. 31, 2024. The other 72.4% is held by investors that do not file the form, including individuals, advisors below the reporting threshold and most investors outside the U.S.


-


**Hedge funds hold less than a fifth, down from half.** The three hedge fund categories together hold 19.0% of 13F-reported holdings, against 50.6% on Dec. 31, 2024. Basis and relative-value funds hold 34,053 BTC-equivalent, down from a peak of 101,826 on Dec. 31, 2024, although they and macro funds were buyers in the quarter (+9,184 and +10,492, respectively).


-


**BlackRock’s IBIT accounts for two-thirds of the institutional position.** Filers hold 232,453 BTC-equivalent of IBIT, 65.2% of everything they reported, and the fund took 34,744 of the quarter's net 49,229. Filers' holdings of GBTC fell for the 10th straight quarter, and its sister fund, the Grayscale Bitcoin Mini Trust, passed it for the first time.


-


**The reported holders are overwhelmingly U.S.-based.** Managers in the U.S. hold a record 293,830 BTC-equivalent, or 82.5% of the 13F-reported total. The share held by managers outside the U.S. fell to 17.5% from 18.6% (the peak was 24.0% on Sept. 30, 2025) even though their holdings rose to 62,456 from 57,274, because U.S. managers added far more.


-


**What the filings cannot show.** A Form 13F reports long positions at the quarter end, and only for accounts over which the manager has investment discretion. Short positions and most derivatives are not reported, so ETP shares held by a market maker or a basis fund may be hedged, and client-directed brokerage accounts are generally absent, so we believe ownership through the wealth channel is understated. The filings are also a snapshot of Sept. 30, 2026. The funds' bitcoin holdings have since fallen by 38,531, to 1,252,139 on Nov. 16, 2026.


## Q3 2026 by the Numbers


For the quarter ended Sept. 30, 2026, 2,166 managers reported 356,491 BTC-equivalent ($29.78 billion) across 13 spot bitcoin funds, 191 more managers than on June 30, 2026. Measured in shares, to exclude the move in the bitcoin price, their net change was +49,229 BTC-equivalent, or about $4.11 billion at quarter-end prices. A total of 358 managers reported a position after holding none a quarter earlier, 167 that had held one reported none, and 1,808 held in both quarters.


### Largest net additions


-


Wells Fargo: +14,636, to 30,553 from 15,931


-


Brevan Howard: +8,606, to 12,686 from 4,082


-


Bank of America: +7,201, to 8,424 from 1,225


-


Millennium Management: +7,114, to 14,516 from 7,417


-


Jane Street: +6,180, to 23,167 from 17,007


### Largest net reductions


-


Walleye Capital: −3,270, to 370 from 3,642


-


Galaxy Digital: −2,721, to 4,786 from 7,519


-


Avenir Tech: −2,274, to 5,396 from 7,675


-


Cantor Fitzgerald: −1,680, to 1,949 from 3,650


-


Bank of Montreal: −1,632, to 1,014 from 2,648


### Largest new holders


-


Balyasny Asset Management: 1,782


-


D. E. Shaw: 1,075


-


SigFig Wealth Management: 884


-


Garda Capital Partners: 625


-


Symmetry Investments: 423


*Figures are BTC-equivalent (see the methodology section for the calculations). They reflect 2,166 filings made through Nov. 17, 2026, the day after the reporting deadline. In past quarters, only 97.7% of filings were in by the end of the deadline day, so late filings and amendments could still move these numbers.*


## How Much Institutions Hold


The charts in this section size the institutional position: its share of all the bitcoin in the funds, the number of managers behind it, and how it divides among the funds in bitcoin, in dollars and as a share of each fund.


### Spot Bitcoin ETP Holdings by 13F Filer Group


The spot bitcoin ETPs held 1,290,670 BTC, worth $107.81 billion, on Sept. 30, 2026. Managers that file Form 13F reported 356,286 of it, or 27.6%, up from 24.8% on June 30, 2026, and just under the high of 27.7% at Dec. 31, 2024. The other 72.4% (934,383 bitcoin) belongs to holders that do not file the form, a group that includes individual investors, advisors below the reporting threshold, and most investors outside the U.S.


The 10 largest filers held 149,388 BTC-equivalent, which is 11.6% of all ETP bitcoin and 41.9% of what filers reported. That concentration was 59.4% on March 31, 2024, and fell as low as 34.2% at March 31, 2026, before large purchases by a few firms lifted it in the latest quarter. The other 2,154 filers held 206,898 (16.0%).


The filings describe Sept. 30, 2026, and the funds have had net outflows since. The dashed line shows their bitcoin falling to 1,252,139 by Nov. 16, 2026, 38,531 below the quarter-end level, while the price of bitcoin fell to $64,943 from $83,580. How filers behaved during that decline will not be known until the next round of filings arrives in February.


### Institutional 13F Filers Holding Spot Bitcoin ETPs


The number of managers reporting a position in at least one spot bitcoin fund rose by 191 to 2,166, the first increase after two quarters of decline. The count is more than double the 1,009 that reported on March 31, 2024, the first quarter end after the funds launched, and is 85 short of the record 2,251 on Dec. 31, 2025.


IBIT, BlackRock's fund, is by far the most widely held, with 1,648 managers, or 76% of all filers, which is 35 managers short of its own peak. GBTC (677), FBTC (665), the Grayscale Bitcoin Mini Trust (511) and BITB (310) follow, and HODL reached a record 138.


Most of these positions are small. Half of the 2,166 managers hold less than 10.4 BTC-equivalent, about $870,000 at the quarter-end price, and 215 hold less than one. The count of managers is therefore a measure of how widely the funds are used, not of how much bitcoin institutions hold.


### BTC-Equivalent Held by 13F Filers by ETP


Filers reported 356,491 BTC-equivalent across the spot funds, the most ever recorded and 2,192 more than the previous high of 354,299 on Sept. 30, 2025. The position has roughly doubled from 175,588 on March 31, 2024.


IBIT accounts for 232,453 of the total, or 65.2%, although that is below the fund's own peak of 240,068 on Sept. 30, 2025. Fidelity’s FBTC is second at 41,429, its highest since June 30, 2025.


The two Grayscale funds continued to move in opposite directions. Filers' holdings of GBTC (one of the oldest vehicles in the space, which converted from a grantor trust to an ETF in 2024) fell for the 10th straight quarter, to 15,842 from 68,449 on March 31, 2024. The lower-fee Grayscale Bitcoin Mini Trust rose for the sixth straight quarter, to 22,382, and for the first time holds more 13F-reported bitcoin than GBTC.


### Quarterly Change in Count of 13F Filers by Fund


The number of managers rose in 12 of the 13 funds, and only BRRR lost holders (two). IBIT gained 152, GBTC 65, the Grayscale Bitcoin Mini Trust 39, FBTC 34 and BITB 34. That reverses the trend of the first half of 2026, when 12 of 13 funds lost managers in Q1 and 10 of 13 in Q2.


Two details help in reading the chart below. The bars for Q3 sum to +390 while the number of distinct managers rose by 191, because a manager that adds a second or third fund counts once for each. And a fund can gain holders while losing bitcoin: GBTC added 65 managers in a quarter when filers reduced their GBTC shares by 5,897 BTC-equivalent.


### New vs. Exiting 13F Holders


This next chart splits the change in the manager count into arrivals and departures. In Q3 2026, 358 managers reported a position after reporting none a quarter earlier, 167 that had held one reported none, and 1,808 held in both quarters, for a net gain of 191.


Both sides improved. Arrivals matched Q4 2025 as the most since Q2 2025 (379) and were more than double the 151 of Q2 2026. Departures were the fewest since Q3 2025 (135), after 316, 335, and 260 in the three quarters before.


The new holders are small. Together they hold 9,554 BTC-equivalent, 2.7% of the total; only 15 of them hold 100 or more, and the median new position is 3.0. Breadth and volume are separate stories in this quarter: the count grew through many small accounts, and the bitcoin was added by a few large ones.


## The Largest Holders


The investment managers’ position in bitcoin ETPs is concentrated. The 10 largest filers hold 42.0% of everything reported, the 25 largest hold 60.8%, and the 50 largest hold 71.2%, so a small number of firms explains most of each quarter's change.


### Largest 13F Holders of U.S. Spot Bitcoin ETPs


Wells Fargo is the largest 13F holder of spot Bitcoin ETPs, with 30,553 BTC-equivalent worth $2.55 billion across 10 funds. That’s up from 15,931 on June 30, 2026. Wells Fargo passed Jane Street (23,167), previously the largest holder. Millennium Management, which ranks fourth with 14,516, had been the largest in every quarter from Q1 2024 through Q1 2026.


The 15 largest holders are a cross-section of the institutional market. Three are wealth platforms (Wells Fargo, Morgan Stanley, and Bank of America), five are market makers or bank trading desks (Jane Street, Goldman Sachs, Marex, Susquehanna, and JPMorgan Chase), three are hedge funds (Millennium Management, Brevan Howard, and Schonfeld), two are asset managers (Horizon Kinetics and BlackRock), one is a sovereign investor (Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala) and one is in the family office or corporate holder category (Avenir Tech). That mix matters for interpretation. The same number of shares can be a client allocation at a wealth platform, inventory at a market maker, or one leg of a hedged trade at a hedge fund, and a bank can hold all three under one filing.


### Top 25 Holders and Their Quarterly Change


The 25 largest holders reported 216,629 BTC-equivalent, 60.8% of the total. Of the 25, 17 added to their positions, six reduced and two made no change. Together they added a net 56,922, more than the 49,229 added by all 2,166 filers.


The green segments show where the bitcoin came from. Wells Fargo added 14,636 (to 30,553 from 15,931), Brevan Howard 8,606 (to 12,686 from 4,082), Bank of America 7,201 (to 8,424 from 1,225), Millennium Management 7,114, Jane Street 6,180, Goldman Sachs 5,499, and Susquehanna 4,839. Those seven firms added 54,076 between them.


The largest reductions among the 25 were at Galaxy Digital (2,721), Avenir Tech (2,274), and NEOS Investment Management (939). (Note that some firms may have adjusted how they hold exposure, such as by switching between spot, ETPs, or derivatives, depending on market circumstances and strategy). Mubadala (8,336) and Abu Dhabi Investment Council (4,653), both Abu Dhabi sovereign investors, reported no change.


### Top 50 Holders and Net Quarterly Change


The next chart widens the lens to capture the 50 largest holders, which together hold 71.2% of the total, and plots only the change. Of the 50, 30 added, 15 reduced and five were unchanged, for a net addition of 59,578 BTC-equivalent.


All filers together added 49,229, so every other manager combined, including the 167 that left, was a net seller of 10,349. Managers that closed their positions account for about 7,689 of that reduction, and the 2,116 current holders ranked below the top 50 for about 2,660. The quarter's accumulation was the work of a few dozen large institutions; the long tail of smaller holders, taken together, did not add.


Two of the 50 are new holders: Balyasny Asset Management (1,782) and D. E. Shaw (1,075), both classified here as basis and relative-value hedge funds. D. E. Shaw returned, having been among the 10 largest holders on Dec. 31, 2024. Below the top 25, the larger additions came from IMC (+1,550), Citigroup (+1,524), and Graham Capital Management (+1,048) and the larger reductions from Cantor Fitzgerald (−1,680) and Laurore (−906).


## Who the Holders Are


The charts in this section sort every filer into one of eight holder types and follow each type's holdings and flows. This is where the quarter's main story sits. Advisors and wealth platforms, the category that covers RIAs, wealth managers, wirehouses and broker-dealer platforms, are the largest holder type by a wide margin and have been the steadiest buyers since the funds launched. Hedge funds, which held half of all 13F-reported ETP bitcoin at the end of 2024, hold less than a fifth.


We believe the distinction matters because different investor types hold the funds for different reasons. A Form 13F reports long positions only, so the shares held by a basis fund or a market maker may be offset by futures or options that the form does not show. Holdings at advisors are more likely to be unhedged allocations in client accounts. The table below gives the category's record quarter by quarter.


### Quarterly Bitcoin-Equivalent Holdings by Holder Type


Advisors and wealth platforms reported 144,307 BTC-equivalent on Sept. 30, 2026, the most in the series and 3.3x the 44,053 they held at March 31, 2024. Their holdings have grown in each of the last nine quarters. The only decline in the series is Q2 2024, when the category fell to 40,155. That decline came entirely from wirehouses and broker-dealer platforms, whose holdings fell to 6,065 from 14,755; independent RIAs and wealth managers added in the same quarter.


The category has been the largest holder type since Q3 2025. Before that it was basis and relative-value hedge funds, whose holdings peaked at 101,826 on Dec. 31, 2024, and have fallen by about two-thirds since, to 34,053.


Market makers and bank desks rank second at a record 77,769. Asset managers (41,211) came in third, followed by basis and relative-value hedge funds (34,053), other hedge funds and crypto firms (16,933), macro hedge funds (16,656), pensions, sovereigns and endowments (16,545), and family offices and corporates (8,812). The decline at asset managers, from 42,361, is the first for that type.


### Share of 13F Holdings by Holder Type


This next chart restates the same holdings as shares of the total, which makes the change in the holder base easier to see. Advisors and wealth platforms hold 40.5% of 13F-reported spot Bitcoin ETP holdings, the highest in the series, against 24.3% a year earlier and 25.1% on March 31, 2024.


The share has risen for five straight quarters, from 22.2% at June 30, 2025. It did not rise in every quarter before that. It fell in Q2 2024, when the wirehouses reduced, and again in Q4 2024 and Q2 2025, when advisors were buying but hedge funds and trading firms were buying more. Measured against all the bitcoin in the funds, including the part that no 13F filer reports, the category holds 11.2%, up from 5.3% on March 31, 2024, and that share has risen for nine straight quarters.


The three hedge fund categories together hold 19.0%, down from a peak of 50.6% on Dec. 31, 2024. Basis and relative-value funds alone shrunk from 33.9% on March 31, 2024, to 9.6%. Market makers and bank desks have stayed between 16.8% and 23.7% throughout and held 21.8% at quarter end.


### Net Quarterly Change by Holder Type


The next chart isolates Q3 2026. Five of the eight holder types added and three reduced. Advisors and wealth platforms (+24,838) accounted for 50.5% of the +49,176 added by all filers across the 12 exchange-listed products, ahead of market makers and bank desks (+14,600), macro hedge funds (+10,492) and basis and relative-value hedge funds (+9,184). Pensions, sovereigns, and endowments were close to flat (+181).


The types that reduced were other hedge funds and crypto firms (−5,295), family offices and corporates (−3,798,) and asset managers (−1,024). For family offices and corporates, it was the third straight quarterly reduction, and for asset managers it was the first net reduction in the series.


One qualification applies to the largest bar. The advisor category includes the wirehouses, and the wirehouse unit breakdown table shows that their dealer and trading units, which behave more like the market makers and bank desks in the second bar, rose to 12,551 BTC-equivalent from 3,982 during the quarter.


### Table of Net Quarterly Change by Holder Type (BTC-equivalent)


The table below gives the numbers behind the holder type charts above and splits several holder types into their components. Three patterns stand out.


First, among advisors and wealth platforms, the buying has shifted from independent firms to the large platforms. RIAs and wealth managers added in nine of the 10 quarters and account for 51,567 of the category's cumulative 100,003, but their flows in 2026 have been small (+2,492, −1,565, and +2,110). Wirehouses and broker-dealer platforms have added for nine straight quarters and at a rising pace: 3,998 in Q1 2026, 11,953 in Q2 2026 and 22,728 in Q3 2026.


Second, basis and relative-value hedge funds are the only holder type with a negative cumulative total (−25,365). They have sold more since March 31, 2024, than they bought.


Third, sovereign wealth and government holders added 13,142 between Q4 2024 and Q1 2026 and have not reported a net reduction in any quarter. They hold 13,101.


### Wirehouses and Broker-Dealer Platform Holdings by Business Unit


A bank or brokerage files one Form 13F for many subsidiaries, so a wirehouse's total can combine client accounts at its advisor arm with positions on its trading desk. This table uses each filing's own list of included managers to separate them.


The 19 firms in the group hold 63,858 BTC-equivalent ($5.34 billion), up from 41,202 on June 30, 2026. Of that, 43,583 sits at advisor and brokerage arms, 12,551 at dealer and trading units, 5,256 at banks and trust companies, and 2,468 at asset management and other units.


Holdings at the advisor and brokerage arms rose 41% in the quarter, from 30,978, so the main finding holds: the wealth channel itself is adding. But dealer and trading units more than tripled, to 12,551 from 3,982, and the advisor arms' share of the group fell to 68.2% from 75.2%. Counting only RIAs and these advisor arms, the wealth channel holds 124,032 BTC-equivalent, up from 109,548. That is more than the whole advisor category held at any earlier quarter end, though as a share of 13F holdings it slipped to 34.8% from 35.6%.


Three firms hold 83.5% of the group's total. Wells Fargo's 30,553 is 85.1% at its advisor and brokerage arms (26,016, up from 13,219). Morgan Stanley's 14,354 is divided among advisor arms (7,141), dealer units (4,925) and asset management and other units (2,288). Bank of America is the exception. Of its 8,424, 7,626 sits at dealer and trading units, up from 421, and 16 at its advisor arms. We would read its increase as dealer positioning, not as demand from wealth clients.


Form 13F covers only assets over which a manager has investment discretion. Client-directed brokerage accounts are generally not in these figures, so they understate what the firms' clients own.


## Where the Holders Are


The next charts place each manager at its principal office. A global bank or wirehouse counts at its headquarters, so this is a map of where the managers are, not of where their clients live. And because a manager outside the U.S. files Form 13F only if it manages at least $100 million in U.S.-listed securities, the figures for managers outside the U.S. are a floor.


### Spot Bitcoin ETP Holdings of 13F Filers by Manager Region


Managers based in the U.S. hold 293,830 BTC-equivalent, 82.5% of the 13F-reported total and the most in the series. Managers outside the U.S. hold 62,456, or 17.5%, across 111 firms.


The U.K. and Crown Dependencies are the largest region outside the U.S. at 25,550, up from 16,699 on June 30, 2026, but about half the peak of 50,138 on Sept. 30, 2025. Asia-Pacific (14,938) has declined for three straight quarters from a peak of 24,353. The Middle East (14,525) is at a record and is the only region that has added in each of the last eight quarters. Canada (2,633), offshore financial centers (2,520), Europe outside the U.K. (2,000), and Latin America (290) are small.


### Net Accumulation per Quarter by Manager Region


U.S. managers added a net 43,961 BTC-equivalent in Q3 2026, their largest quarterly addition since Q4 2024 and 89% of the quarter's total.


The U.K. and Crown Dependencies added 8,850, the region's first net addition after three quarters in which it sold a combined 33,338. The turn is largely one firm: Brevan Howard, which is placed in Jersey, added 8,606. The Middle East added 360 and extended its run of net additions to eight quarters. Asia-Pacific (−2,109) and Canada (−1,746) cut the most, and Asia-Pacific has been a net seller for three straight quarters.


The chart also shows that the selling of late 2025 and early 2026 rotated from region to region. In Q4 2025 the U.K. and Crown Dependencies sold 20,206 while Asia-Pacific added 7,136. In Q1 2026 the U.S. sold 23,515. By Q2 2026 the U.S. had turned buyer (+13,494) while the U.K. and Crown Dependencies and Asia-Pacific were still selling.


### Holdings Outside the U.S. by Country


Four jurisdictions hold 76% of the bitcoin reported by managers outside the U.S. The United Arab Emirates is first with 13,842 BTC-equivalent (22.2% of the non-U.S. total), nearly all of it held by two Abu Dhabi sovereign investors. The island of Jersey is second with 13,149 after more than tripling in the quarter, from 4,121, reflecting the addition of Brevan Howard, which is based there. The U.K. (12,399) was little changed. Hong Kong (8,348) fell by about a third, from 12,408, as Avenir Tech and Laurore reduced.


Australia (3,127), Singapore (2,997), Canada (2,633), and the Cayman Islands (2,219) follow. Canada has the most filers of any country outside the U.S. (27) but small positions, and continental Europe is thinly represented, led by Italy (735) and Switzerland (689).


### 13F Holdings in the U.S. by State


Within the U.S., New York dominates. Managers there hold 138,825 BTC-equivalent, 47.2% of the U.S. total and 39.0% of all 13F-reported holdings, because most of the large hedge funds, market makers, banks and asset managers are placed there. The five largest states (New York, California, Illinois, Pennsylvania and Massachusetts) hold 74.3% of the U.S. total.


The quarter's largest moves trace to single firms. California added 14,651 to reach 43,104, an amount almost equal to the addition at Wells Fargo (14,636), which is placed at its San Francisco headquarters. North Carolina more than quadrupled, to 9,794 from 2,315, on Bank of America's addition in Charlotte. Pennsylvania's gain of 5,234 comes largely from Susquehanna (+4,839).


The managers are distributed differently from the bitcoin. California has the most filers (246), followed by New York (190), Texas (131), Florida (129), Pennsylvania (107) and Illinois (100), a spread that reflects where advisory firms are located more than where the largest positions are held.


Conclusion


The most potent takeaway from Q3 is the relentless growth of advisors and wealth platforms as a distribution channel for bitcoin exposure through ETPs. In our October 2023 report[Sizing the Market for a Bitcoin ETF](https://www.galaxy.com/insights/research/sizing-the-market-for-a-bitcoin-etf) , we argued that the *wealth channel* would be the most important segment for these products.


*The wealth management segment holds significant capital that has been unable to access bitcoin investments directly through traditional channels – with an approved spot ETF, financial advisors can start to direct their wealth clients to invest in bitcoin.*
*Sizing the Market for a Bitcoin ETF.*[Galaxy Research, October 24, 2023](https://www.galaxy.com/insights/research/sizing-the-market-for-a-bitcoin-etf) *.*


Now, more than 3 years later, that channel accounts for 40% of all institutional ownership of these products. The striking growth in Wells Fargo’s reported holdings – 85% of which come from its advisor and broker-dealer platforms – raises the possibility of the enactment of a systematic allocation strategy rather than simply a handful of very bullish clients. Bitcoin ETP holdings in this channel have exclusively increased every quarter since Q2 2024 regardless of market conditions. Because these accounts are longer term focused and utilize a target allocation per asset class in a portfolio, advisors are likely to buy when assets decline in value and sell when they appreciate, contributing to lower volatility and dampening downturns. We expect ETP ownership growth from this segment to continue.


## Appendix: Definitions and Methodology


### What is Form 13F?


Institutional managers with investment discretion over at least $100 million in U.S.-listed equities and other Section 13(f) securities report their holdings to the Securities and Exchange Commission within 45 days of each quarter end. Filings for the quarter ended Sept. 30, 2026, were due Nov. 16, 2026. This report reflects 2,166 filings made through Nov. 17, 2026. In past quarters 97.7% of filings were in by the end of the deadline day, so late filings and amendments can still change the figures.


### What the form does not show


A Form 13F lists long positions at the quarter end. Short positions and most derivatives are not reported, and options positions are excluded here, so a long position at a market maker or a basis fund may be hedged. Only accounts over which the manager has investment discretion are reported, so client-directed accounts are generally absent. A parent and its sub-adviser can both report the same shares.


### What is BTC-equivalent?


A manager's shares in each fund multiplied by the fund's bitcoin per share at the quarter end. For six funds, the rate is equal to the trust's own reported bitcoin divided by its shares outstanding; for seven it is net asset value per share divided by the quarter-end price of bitcoin.


### Net change


The change in a manager's shares from the prior quarter end multiplied by the current quarter's bitcoin per share, adjusted for the share splits in ARKB, HODL and the Grayscale Bitcoin Mini Trust. A move in the price of bitcoin therefore produces no net change. Dollar flows value the same share change at quarter-end share prices.


### Two sets of funds


Several charts and summary figures cover all 13 spot Bitcoin funds that filers reported, including the Osprey Bitcoin Trust, which trades over the counter (2,166 managers; 356,491 BTC-equivalent). Other charts cover the 12 exchange-listed funds (2,164 managers; 356,286 BTC-equivalent).


### Holder types


Each filing manager is assigned to one of eight types from its name, its Form ADV client mix, and a manual review of the largest filers. Wirehouses and broker-dealer platforms are counted with advisors and wealth platforms. We divide their holdings by business unit using the list of other included managers on each filing's cover page and the unit number on each line of its information table.


### New and exiting holders


A new holder reported a spot bitcoin fund at the quarter end and none at the prior quarter end. An exiting holder reported one at the prior quarter end and none at this one.


### Geography


Each manager is placed at its principal office, taken from the filing's cover page and other regulatory records, with registered-agent and mailbox addresses resolved by hand. A global bank or wirehouse counts at its headquarters.


*Primary data source: Galaxy Research, from Form 13F filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission and each fund's published holdings.*
